title: Bridge and Flyweight Patterns
summary: Two less-common but still-asked structural patterns: decoupling an abstraction from its implementation, and sharing state across many objects to cut memory.

slides.markdown:
This topic covers two structural patterns less common in interviews than Adapter or Decorator, but still asked: **Bridge** decouples an abstraction from its implementation so each can vary independently, and **Flyweight** shares immutable state across many objects to cut memory usage.

They don't build on each other — treat them as two short, focused lessons back to back. Bridge answers "how do I avoid an exploding hierarchy when two dimensions both vary?" Flyweight answers "how do I represent millions of similar objects without running out of memory?"

slides.sectionTitle: Bridge: decoupling an abstraction from its implementation so both vary independently
slides.markdown:
Say you have shapes (`Circle`, `Square`) that each need to render via different backends (`VectorRenderer`, `RasterRenderer`). Without Bridge, you'd subclass every combination — `VectorCircle`, `RasterCircle`, `VectorSquare`, `RasterSquare` — and every new shape or renderer multiplies the count.

Bridge splits this into two independent hierarchies connected by composition: a `Shape` abstraction holds a reference to a `Renderer` implementation and delegates the actual drawing to it. Add a new shape, or a new renderer, and you write exactly one new class — not one per combination.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: Bridge separating a Shape abstraction from a Renderer implementation
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: two parallel hierarchies side by side — left column Shape, Circle, Square; right column Renderer, VectorRenderer, RasterRenderer — with a horizontal 'has-a' arrow from Shape to Renderer showing composition bridging the two independent hierarchies >>>

The two hierarchies never inherit from each other — the only connection is the `has-a` arrow. Either side can grow without touching the other.

Flyweight: sharing immutable state across many objects to cut memory
slides.markdown:
A text editor holding a million characters, each as its own object with a font, size, and color, would waste enormous memory storing the same font/size/color combination redundantly a million times. **Flyweight** splits an object's state into **intrinsic** state (shared, immutable — the glyph shape for the letter 'a' in Arial 12pt) and **extrinsic** state (unique per instance — its position on the page), storing only one shared instance per distinct intrinsic combination.

Instead of a million glyph objects, you might have a few hundred shared ones, each reused across every position that happens to need that exact letter/font/size combination.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: shared intrinsic state vs per-object extrinsic state
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a small pool of 3 shared Glyph flyweight objects labeled 'a-Arial-12', 'b-Arial-12', 'c-Arial-12' on the left, with arrows fanning out to many Position objects on the right (each holding x/y coordinates and a reference back to one shared glyph), illustrating many extrinsic contexts pointing at few shared intrinsic objects >>>

The glyph objects on the left never change and are reused everywhere that letter appears. The position objects on the right are cheap, numerous, and hold only what's unique per occurrence.

Compare: Bridge vs Adapter — designed upfront vs retrofitted
slides.markdown:
Both separate an abstraction from an implementation, but the timing and intent differ.

| | Bridge | Adapter |
|---|---|---|
| When decided | Upfront — designed in before either side exists | Retrofitted — added after an incompatible interface already exists |
| Who controls both sides | You control both the abstraction and the implementation | You typically don't control the adaptee |
| Goal | Let two hierarchies vary independently | Make one existing thing fit an interface it wasn't built for |
| Motivation | Avoiding a combinatorial class explosion | Compatibility |

**How to decide:** if you're designing two things that need to vary independently from day one, it's Bridge; if you're bolting a fix onto something that already exists and doesn't match, it's [Adapter](adapter-pattern).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: Flyweight sharing mutable state by mistake, causing cross-talk bugs
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just add a `color` field to the shared Glyph object for convenience — I can update it per use."

**Why it's wrong:** the whole premise of Flyweight is that shared instances are immutable and safe to reuse. If `color` becomes mutable on the shared `Glyph`, changing it for one occurrence of the letter 'a' silently changes every other occurrence sharing that pooled instance — a cross-talk bug that's brutal to trace, since unrelated text appears to randomly change color.

**Correct model:** anything that varies per occurrence — color, position, selection state — is extrinsic and must live outside the shared flyweight, passed in as a parameter, never as mutable state on the pooled object itself.
